cards.title: Ego Appeal Through Envious Comparison
cards.summary: Show the buyer's peers envying them to trigger ego-driven purchase desire for premium products.
cards.use_when: Creating acquisition creative or PDP imagery for a premium, status-signalling product where the buyer's self-image drives the purchase.
steps: Identify whether your product is a 'trophy' purchase where visible ownership signals taste, success or status (luxury car, high-end gear, designer goods).

Build the scene around the buyer or owner being admired or envied by an equal-status peer, not just the product in isolation — the Rolls-Royce example shows a Mercedes driver squirming with envy at the stoplight.
Keep the peer plausibly the buyer's equal so the comparison stings; the Mercedes driver has status but less than the Rolls owner, which makes the desired upgrade feel attainable.
Note this is a peripheral-route cue: it works when purchase motivation is emotional and identity-based, per the source.
caveats: The source explicitly states not all products suit ego appeal; it fits status goods, not functional commodities.
The envy framing is the author's illustrative advertisement example, not a tested benchmark.

cards.title: Transfer: Borrow Credibility From Respected Symbols
cards.summary: Use trusted institutional symbols, seals and expert cues so buyers question your sales argument less.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, landing pages or ad creative for products where prospect skepticism — not awareness — is the main conversion blocker.
steps: Diagnose whether the real problem is disbelief: the source's frustrated advertiser had a good layout, photo, price and easy ordering but no sales because nobody believed him.
Identify people, groups or institutions your buyers already respect (medical bodies, professional guilds, national agencies, science, the Church, industry associations).
Get an official endorsement, testimonial or membership credential and then get permission to use their image, logo or a short video on your site or ads.

If a full endorsement is unavailable, spotlight recognized symbols that carry endorsement weight — the source cites the Good Housekeeping Seal of Approval and the official-looking logo of the National Guild of Hypnotists on a client's postcard.
Add authoritative-looking facts, figures and scientific-style graphs alongside the symbol to reinforce the transferred credibility.
Where relevant, surface an actual guarantee the trusted group stands behind; the Good Housekeeping seal promised refund or replacement within two years and functioned as a close-the-sale inducement.
caveats: The source notes many prospects use peripheral, non-critical thinking; if the purchase is high-cost and central-route, credibility cues alone are insufficient.
The hypnotist postcard example is an anecdote; the author states most recipients had never heard of the guild yet the credibility cue still functioned.

cards.title: Bandwagon Effect: Link Products to Reference Groups
cards.summary: Persuade buyers by tying your product to aspirational, associative or dissociative reference groups they identify with.
cards.use_when: Choosing models, testimonials or lifestyle imagery for acquisition creative and brand positioning.
steps: Decide which of the three reference groups you are targeting: aspirational (groups the buyer wants to join), associative (groups sharing their ideals), or dissociative (groups they want to reject).

For aspirational influence, ensure prospects can easily identify with the people shown — match age and profile. For a racing bike-seat product with a median buyer age of 34, the source advises showing tour-winning pros like Lance Armstrong or Eddy Merckx, not elderly riders, casual 'Everyday Joe' riders, or your best-paying customer who isn't aspirational to the audience.

For associative influence, either appeal directly to the group's values in your creative, or disassociate from outside groups (the source cites the Gap's 'generation gap' name and youth-culture versus 'oldies' appeal), being aware you will alienate the groups you reject.
Choose your group axis: age, class, sex, geography, politics, education.
Write copy and imagery that tells buyers how buying makes them part of, keeps them in, or visibly distances them from a group — not just what features the product has.
caveats: The source cites Stec and Bernstein's Consensus-Implies-Correctness heuristic and Cialdini's comparison cues as support, but the store-specific lift is not quantified.
Dissociative framing offends the rejected group by design; judge whether alienating them damages your market.

cards.title: Means-End Chain: Sell the Benefit of the Benefit
cards.summary: Write copy and imagery that points to the ultimate end result, so buyers evaluate the outcome instead of scrutinizing the product.
cards.use_when: Drafting PDP copy, hero headlines or ad hooks when the product's raw features are unremarkable or commodity-like.
steps: Run the source's 'why' chain on your product: 'The sign tells people who you are' → so they do business with you → so you sell products → so you make money. Keep asking 'what's the benefit of that?' until you reach the buyer's ultimate value.

Write copy and select images that always represent that positive end result, not the intermediate step: shovel buyers want attractive planted gardens, microwave buyers want time back, car buyers want to get from A to B with ego appeal as icing.
Shift the copy's focus so prospects are less likely to critically analyse product pros and cons and more likely to decide on the outcome it delivers.
Apply the Lexus example as a template: rather than selling the car's feel, sell that a realtor driving it looks more successful and therefore wins more listings.
caveats: The Lexus example comes from a fictional salesman's pitch, not a measured campaign; it is an illustration of the technique.
The source notes ego appeal is a layer on top of the core benefit, not a substitute for it.

cards.title: Match Ad Content to Buyer Stage (Transtheoretical Model)
cards.summary: Identify whether prospects are unaware, considering, planning, buying or habitual, then write copy for that stage.
cards.use_when: Planning a campaign series, email flow or landing page for a product with varying buyer awareness.
steps: Classify your market using the source's five stages: Precontemplation (ignorant of your product or unaware they need it), Contemplation (aware and thinking about trying it), Preparation (planning, needs benefit/price detail), Action (ready to buy), Maintenance (regular repurchase).
Recognise your audience will be spread across stages at the same time.

Choose option one: write ads covering all five stages so each prospect finds their relevant chunk — include everything someone totally unfamiliar would need, including what it is, what's in it, why it's better and what it costs.
Choose option two: run a series of ads that progresses from stage one to stage five over time, each building on the last with increasing feature and benefit depth.
Match copy density to the stage: stage-one prospects need an introduction, stage-three prospects need benefit and advantage detail, stage-four prospects need a frictionless purchase path.
Reinforce existing attitudes where possible — the source states it is far easier to reinforce current behaviour than to change values.
caveats: Stage bands are a source-cited model (Prochaska 1994) applied to advertising; they are not a measurement system for your funnel.
The source does not give numeric thresholds for how many prospects sit in each stage.

cards.title: Inoculation Theory: Pre-empt Competitors' Attacks
cards.summary: Warn prospects about competitors' claims and weak arguments in advance so they compare purchases through your filter.
cards.use_when: Writing comparison content, objection-handling copy or competitor-differentiation sections on PDPs and landing pages.
steps: Follow the source's three steps: (1) warn of an impending attack, (2) make a weak attack, (3) encourage a strong defence by prompting the prospect to articulate their own position.

Use the pizza example as a copy template: 'Our competitors tell you they use fresh mozzarella, but they don't tell you they buy it pre-shredded in bags; we hand-shred ours every morning.' Repeat the tell-you / don't-tell-you pattern for dough, delivery time and guarantees.
Take the consumer-advocate position and expose what to look out for, what's good, what's bad and what's suspect in your category, implying enough confidence to invite closer inspection.
Turn competitor criticisms of your brand into weak attacks your own copy answers, as the source notes advertisers do to reinforce loyalty.
Keep the attack weak; the source warns a strong attack risks weakening or reversing the prospect's attitude instead of hardening it.
caveats: The source insists the attack must be weak — overreaching can backfire.
This only works if your claims are legitimate; the source ties the technique's goodwill payoff to providing genuinely useful information.
An auto-body shop and pizza shop example are author illustrations, not measured results.

cards.title: Belief Re-ranking: Change Beliefs Without Triggering Defensiveness
cards.summary: Change importance of beliefs or offer alternative evidence rather than telling buyers they're wrong.
cards.use_when: Writing copy to shift buyers off a habit or incumbent brand onto your product without triggering reactance.
steps: Choose between two routes: change the buyer's underlying beliefs by presenting emotional images (fear, humour, guilt) or factual evidence, or change the importance of beliefs they already hold.
Prefer reinforcing or undermining an existing belief over a wholesale change — the source states this is easier and more likely to succeed, and is the more popular persuasion strategy.

Reinforce a belief buyers already hold by adding supporting stats, reports, studies and testimonials, or everyday success stories they can identify with. Health-food advertisers add health-benefit claims to the healthy-diet belief the audience already holds.
Avoid head-on collision: instead of stating 'Milk is healthier than soda', present graphic factual evidence of soda's risks and milk's benefits side by side.
Aim for cognitive dissonance resolution — prospects amend beliefs to fit new perceptions — but accept that some will reject the ad outright; the source notes a 100% response rate is not realistic.
caveats: Prospects must remain unaware they're being influenced; the source states they should believe the decision is their own so it becomes cemented.
The baking soda toothpaste and kung fu examples show belief change over time, not a single-ad effect.

cards.title: Elaboration Likelihood Model: Choose Central or Peripheral Copy
cards.summary: Match ad content to the buyer's thinking depth — heavy facts for high-consideration purchases, image and cues for low-stakes ones.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much evidence and data versus imagery and celebrity cues to put into a PDP, ad or landing page.
steps: Judge whether your product needs high personal relevance thinking (costly or important) or low-involvement processing (cheap, trivial, routine). A $928,000 house versus a can of pork and beans is the source's contrast.
For central-route products, pour on facts, stats, evidence, testimonials, studies, reports and case histories woven into the sales argument.
For peripheral-route products, load ads with colourful pleasant images, humour, popular subject matter or celebrity sponsorship — but still include fundamental data.

Even for low-involvement goods, state size, colour, weight, quantity and any measurable specification (the source cites TAPPI brightness rating for inkjet paper), and explicitly say how you're better than competitors.

Expect the payoff to differ: the source states central-route attitudes are more resistant to counter-persuasion and show greater attitude-behaviour consistency, while peripheral-route attitudes are easily changed.
caveats: The best route depends on the product; the source says don't use cues-heavy creative for luxury or high-cost items.
The distinction is the author's synthesis of the ELM, and the house/beans examples are illustrations rather than test data.

cards.title: Cialdini's Six Cues (CLARCCS) for Peripheral-Route Ads
cards.summary: Deploy comparison, liking, authority, reciprocation, commitment/consistency and scarcity as mental shortcuts in low-consideration ad copy.
cards.use_when: Writing acquisition creative or PDP persuasion blocks for low-cost or impulse purchases where buyers won't deliberate deeply.
steps: Comparison: signal that a buyer's peers are already choosing your product ('everybody else is doing it'), leaning on the need to belong.

Liking: use likable spokespeople, ad characters or relatable users; the source notes the lynchpin is that the buyer must like the person, whether a catalog seller, a celebrity or a friend who bought before.

Authority: use official, intelligent or expert figures to endorse; the source notes actors who played doctors on TV still persuaded viewers even after being made to say 'I'm not really a doctor' — the cue survived disclosure.
Reciprocation: give something of value first (samples, gift certificates, free trials, even a dollar with a survey) so buyers feel obligated to return the favour.
Commitment/consistency and scarcity: use consistency pressure and limited availability to push compliance.

Use attractive faces in creative: the source cites research (Down & Lyons 1991) that attractive people are judged more trustworthy and likable, and notes men respond to pictures of men and women to pictures of women because of identification.
caveats: The source states these cues should not be your main tool when the purchase requires lots of thought, such as luxury or high-ticket items.
The author cautions against valuing the free gift cheaply — for reciprocation, give something of real value, not a junky logo key ring.

cards.title: Reciprocation Offers That Kickstart Purchase
cards.summary: Give genuine value up front to create obligation and start the reciprocation loop toward a paid purchase.
cards.use_when: Designing first-order incentives, new-mover or new-customer offers, samples or lead magnets.
steps: Identify a free item of real value your buyer would want: a free entrée, free oil change or discount certificate rather than a disposable trinket.
Time it to a moment of need — the source cites Moving Targets sending gift certificates to people who just moved into a neighbourhood on behalf of restaurant and auto-shop clients.
Deliver the free experience well; the source notes that if the customer was treated right and was satisfied, they are far more likely to return and become a loyal long-term customer.
Consider offering to a named local partner or audience segment so the gift also introduces your business.
Judge the giveaway against the source's warning: don't use junky, low-value items with just a logo and phone number — give something of value.
caveats: The source frames reciprocation as compelling but does not quantify return rates.
Moving Targets is a client example, not evidence your store will see the same conversion.
